mcqs.question: Why can't Ansible replace Terraform in a typical pipeline, even though both are IaC tools?
options: Ansible is strictly older and less capable software
Ansible only works with on-premises hardware
Ansible is a configuration-management tool for existing machines, not a provisioning tool for creating cloud infrastructure
Terraform and Ansible are actually interchangeable for every use case
mcqs.explanation: Ansible's job is configuring what runs on a machine that already exists (packages, files, services) — it has no native model for creating the VM/VPC/load balancer itself. Terraform provisions the infrastructure Ansible then configures; they solve different, complementary problems rather than one replacing the other.

mcqs.question: What's the key trade-off Pulumi makes by using general-purpose languages instead of a domain-specific language like HCL?
options: It removes the need for a plan/diff step
It loses the ability to manage state entirely
It only supports a single cloud provider
It gains full language power (loops, functions, tests) at the cost of being easier to write something overly clever and hard to reason about
mcqs.explanation: General-purpose languages bring real programming constructs and existing tooling (unit tests, IDE support), but that same expressiveness makes it easier to write infrastructure logic that's clever but hard to predict — the opposite trade-off from HCL's deliberately constrained simplicity. Pulumi still tracks state and supports multiple providers, and still has a preview/diff step analogous to plan.

mcqs.question: What actually happens when AWS CDK code is deployed?
options: CDK synthesizes a CloudFormation template from the code, and CloudFormation applies that template -- CDK itself is a code generator, not a separate execution engine
CDK talks directly to AWS service APIs, bypassing CloudFormation entirely
CDK code compiles into Terraform HCL before being applied
CDK requires Pulumi to be installed as its execution backend
mcqs.explanation: CDK's mechanism is synthesis: your TypeScript/Python/Java code generates a CloudFormation template, and CloudFormation itself does the actual provisioning. This is the key architectural difference from Pulumi, which talks to provider APIs through its own engine rather than generating another tool's template format.

mcqs.question: Why does an IaC tool choice deserve more weight than most tooling decisions?
options: Migrating thousands of existing resources to a different tool's state model later means importing each one individually and re-verifying nothing changes -- effectively a rewrite, not a config change
IaC tools are all functionally identical, so the choice doesn't actually matter
Cloud providers only support one IaC tool per account
Switching IaC tools requires destroying and recreating all existing infrastructure
mcqs.explanation: The cost is import/reconciliation effort across every existing resource, not necessarily destruction and recreation -- but that's still substantial, ongoing work that compounds as more resources are added under the original tool. Providers don't restrict which IaC tool manages an account, and the tools are meaningfully different in model and trade-offs.

mcqs.question: An org ends up running Terraform, CDK, and Pulumi across three different teams, none of whom coordinated the choice. What's the actual problem worth fixing?
options: Multiple IaC tools are always strictly forbidden and must be consolidated immediately
The tools themselves are incompatible and none of them will actually work correctly
Nothing needs to change, since each team's individual choice was locally reasonable

The lack of a deliberate, platform-level decision -- not necessarily the plurality of tools itself -- which leaves the org without a shared source of truth and a permanent multiplier on onboarding and incident cost
mcqs.explanation: A genuine trade-off can justify more than one tool, so the fix isn't automatically forcing one everywhere -- it's making the choice deliberate and reviewed rather than something each team backs into independently, since the compounding cost is coordination and expertise spread thin, not a technical incompatibility between the tools.
